articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This action aims to disrupt illicit networks that pose a threat to international security.

These designations are part of a broader effort by the U.S. government to combat global illicit finance and prevent terrorist organizations and drug traffickers from accessing the international financial system. The specific individuals and entities targeted were not detailed in the initial announcement but are expected to be identified on the SDN list.

The move underscores the U.S.'s commitment to leveraging its sanctions authorities to protect national security interests and those of its allies by cutting off financial support to dangerous actors worldwide.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran-Related SDN Listing for Volta Shipping Services LLC
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an update to an Iran-related listing on its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List on November 9, 2026. The update pertains to Volta Shipping Services LLC, a UAE-based company previously linked to Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani.

The key change in this update is the alteration of Volta Shipping Services LLC's listed alias from Volta Shipping Services FZCO to Volta Container Line FZCO. The company remains designated under Executive Order 13902, which targets Iran's proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and its support for terrorism.

This administrative update reinforces the ongoing scrutiny of entities involved in Iran's shipping sector and highlights the U.S. government's efforts to maintain accurate and current sanctions lists to prevent evasion.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Eight Canada-Based Money Services Businesses Tied to Iran's Digital Asset Sector
body: On November 6, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) imposed blocking sanctions on eight Canada-based money services businesses (MSBs) for facilitating transactions involving Iran. These businesses are accused of operating within Iran's digital asset sector, including converting Iranian currency into digital assets and conducting transactions with sanctioned Iranian exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' and coordinated with FinCEN and Canada's FINTRAC, was taken under Executive Order 13902. It specifically targets international financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions and fund its illicit activities.

The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting Iran's access to the global financial system, particularly through emerging technologies like digital assets, and serves as a warning to other entities that might facilitate such evasion.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Expands Cuba Sanctions
body: On November 5, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new Cuba designations. This action included sanctioning four individuals and 41 entities linked to the Cambodia-based Prince Group transnational criminal organization (Prince Group TCO) for their involvement in global scam networks.

Separately, OFAC designated Malaysian national Chui Kok Wa, identified as the leader of a Madagascar-based scam network that defrauded U.S. victims of over $400,000 through cyber-enabled schemes. This designation was made under cyber-related sanctions authorities.

Concurrently, the U.S. issued a determination expanding sanctions on Cuba, paving the way for restrictions on the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy. This move also targeted a crude oil shipping network, state-owned entities, and China-based suppliers of Cuba's military forces.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Herbert Smith Freehills

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Alert on Shadow Fleet, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: On November 4, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and published an alert warning of the Iranian shadow fleet's reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion. The designations targeted five individuals and ten entities in India, Singapore, and Turkey for their support of Iran's maritime and aviation sectors.

Specifically, OFAC sanctioned an India-based network led by Suniel Kumar Sharma and Jaspreet Preeti Shahid for providing false flags and certifications to vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, including those operating on behalf of the Iranian military. Turkey-based Fugo Ground Services Inc. was also sanctioned for supporting Iran's aviation sector.

Additionally, OFAC issued Venezuela-related General License 5AA, replacing General License 5Z, which authorizes certain transactions related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 percent bond on or after December 18, 2026. An amended Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 595) was also published.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Treasury OFAC

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: On October 29, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License. The specific details of the amendments were not immediately released but are typically aimed at clarifying or adjusting authorized activities under existing sanctions programs.

General Licenses are crucial for providing humanitarian aid, facilitating certain types of trade, or allowing for specific transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under comprehensive sanctions regimes. Amendments often reflect evolving policy considerations or address practical implementation challenges.
This action indicates OFAC's ongoing management and refinement of its Iran sanctions program, ensuring that the measures remain effective while allowing for legitimate activities.

body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities and individuals related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions are part of the U.S. government's efforts to counter illicit activities and human rights abuses in these regions.

The North Korea designations likely aim to disrupt the regime's weapons proliferation programs and other destabilizing activities, while the DRC-related designations typically address corruption, human rights abuses, or illicit resource exploitation.
These designations underscore the U.S.'s commitment to using sanctions as a tool to promote accountability and deter harmful conduct by state and non-state actors globally.

These amendments are intended to provide updated guidance and clarity for financial institutions and other entities on their compliance obligations.

The FAQs serve as a critical resource for understanding OFAC's regulations and ensuring proper adherence to sanctions programs. Updates often reflect new enforcement trends, technological changes, or common compliance challenges faced by the private sector.

This action highlights OFAC's ongoing commitment to transparency and assisting the public in navigating the complexities of sanctions compliance, ultimately aiming to enhance the effectiveness of U.S. sanctions policy.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain entities from sanctions lists related to Belarus and North Korea. Additionally, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations continue the U.S. government's pressure campaign against Tehran's illicit activities. The removals for Belarus and North Korea suggest a recalibration of sanctions in those areas, potentially in response to specific actions or policy shifts.

The issuance of new General Licenses for Iran and Russia, along with updated FAQs, aims to provide clarity and facilitate certain transactions under the complex sanctions regimes, indicating a dynamic approach to sanctions implementation.

articles.headline: EU Imposes New Sanctions on 143 Russian Individuals and Entities Over Ukraine War and Hybrid Attacks
body: The European Union on Monday, November 16, 2026, imposed new sanctions on 143 Russian-linked individuals and entities, significantly expanding its restrictive measures against Moscow. This latest package targets key sectors of the Russian economy, including nearly 50 banks and financial institutions, energy companies, oil traders, and organizations accused of conducting cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns.

The sanctions, approved by EU foreign ministers in Brussels, aim to further reduce Russia's ability to finance its war against Ukraine and counter Russian interference across Europe. Among the targeted entities are the owner of the Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries, Tatyana Kim, and an individual controlling a majority stake in rival platform Ozon, Alexander Chachava.

In a separate decision, the EU also sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities, including the Kremlin-backed Social Design Agency (SDA) and the pro-Russian hacker group NoName057(16), for their involvement in disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks targeting EU member states and partner countries. These measures include asset freezes and travel bans for listed individuals, and prohibit EU citizens and companies from making funds available to those sanctioned.
articles.source: Council of the EU / Reuters / The Kyiv Independent

articles.headline: Cubans Protest U.S. Sanctions at Marabana Marathon Amid Deepening Economic Crisis
body: Thousands of participants in Cuba's Marabana international marathon on Sunday, November 15, 2026, used the event to protest U.S. economic sanctions against the island. Many runners wore signs reading 'The blockade is suffocating the Cuban people' and 'Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is,' highlighting the severe impact of the embargo.

New U.S. tariffs on countries supplying oil to Cuba have exacerbated the island's fuel crisis, leading to widespread power outages that disrupt essential services like water, internet, and phone service. This has pushed Cuba deeper into an economic and energy crisis.

The economic strain also affected the marathon itself, with longtime sponsor Adidas withdrawing support this year and other companies, such as Meliá Hotels International, pulling back from the island due to tightening sanctions.

articles.headline: U.S. Bans Imports from Three Chinese Biotech Companies Over Xinjiang Forced Labor Allegations
body: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced on October 29, 2026, a ban on imports from three prominent Chinese biotech companies—BGI Group, BGI Genomics, and MGI Tech—under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA). This action stems from credible information indicating these companies' support for genetic testing in Xinjiang, which facilitates the monitoring, surveillance, and repression of ethnic minorities, including through forced labor.

The companies were added to the UFLPA Entity List, effectively barring their goods from the U.S. market unless importers can provide clear and convincing evidence that the products were not made with forced labor. DHS stated that these firms are either sourcing materials from Xinjiang or collaborating with the regional government to recruit, transport, transfer, harbor, or receive forced labor of persecuted ethnic groups.

This move expands U.S. trade controls into the life sciences sector and underscores the U.S. government's commitment to eradicating ethical violations from corporate supply chains and protecting American businesses from unfair competition. China's Ministry of Commerce has strongly condemned the measure, calling it a pretext for unilateral protectionism.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors, Transfers from USML to EAR
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced last week that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List (USML).

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with the controls already applied to firearms. The move is part of an ongoing effort to streamline and clarify export control regulations, potentially easing the burden on exporters while maintaining national security interests.

Exporters of these items will now need to comply with EAR requirements, which may involve different licensing procedures and classifications compared to the USML. This change is expected to be welcomed by the industry for simplifying the regulatory landscape.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
